stem: Natural vegetation refers to:
options: The plant community that has grown naturally, without human help, and has been left undisturbed for a long time
Only forests planted by the government
solution: Natural vegetation refers to the plant community (plants, trees, shrubs, grasses) that has grown naturally on its own — without any human interference or help — and has been left undisturbed for a long time, so that it has adjusted itself to the natural conditions (climate, soil, etc.) of the area. This is in contrast to cultivated crops or planted gardens (which are grown by humans). The natural vegetation that is truly virgin/undisturbed is also called 'virgin vegetation'. Understanding natural (virgin) vegetation (grown naturally, undisturbed) is a prelims point. Natural vegetation is the plant community that grows naturally, without human help, undisturbed for a long time.

stem: The most important factor determining the type of natural vegetation in a region is:
solution: The most important factor determining the type of natural vegetation in a region is the climate — especially the amount of rainfall and the temperature (and also sunlight and humidity). Different plants need different amounts of water and warmth, so the vegetation of a place reflects its climate: areas of heavy rainfall grow dense forests, areas of moderate rain grow deciduous forests or grasslands, and dry areas grow desert/thorn vegetation. (Other factors — like soil, relief/altitude, and drainage — also influence vegetation, but climate is the chief control.) This is why India's natural vegetation varies with its rainfall/climate. Understanding that climate is the main control of natural vegetation is a prelims point. Climate (especially rainfall and temperature) is the most important factor determining the type of natural vegetation.

stem: The type of forest found in areas of very heavy rainfall (over about 200 cm a year), which is dense, green throughout the year, and multi-layered, is the __________ forest.
solution: The tropical evergreen forest (tropical rainforest) is found in areas of very heavy rainfall — generally over about 200 cm (2000 mm) a year — such as the western slopes of the Western Ghats, the north-eastern states, and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands. These forests are: dense (thick) and multi-layered; evergreen (green throughout the year, because the heavy rain and warmth allow the trees to shed leaves at different times, so the forest never looks bare); and rich in a great variety of tall trees (like rosewood, mahogany, ebony) and other life. Understanding the tropical evergreen forest (very heavy rainfall, dense, always green) is a prelims point. Tropical evergreen (rainforest) grows in areas of very heavy rainfall (over ~200 cm), and is dense and green all year.

stem: The most widespread type of forest in India, found in areas of moderate rainfall (about 70–200 cm), whose trees shed their leaves in the dry season, is the __________ forest.
solution: The tropical deciduous forest (also called the monsoon forest) is the most widespread type of forest in India. It is found in areas of moderate rainfall (about 70–200 cm a year). Its trees are 'deciduous' — they shed (drop) their leaves for a few weeks in the dry season (to conserve water). Because they are so widespread and useful, these are the most economically important forests of India, and they include valuable timber trees like teak, sal, sandalwood, and sheesham. They are divided into moist deciduous (higher rainfall) and dry deciduous (lower rainfall) forests. Understanding the tropical deciduous (monsoon) forest — the most widespread in India — is a key prelims point. The tropical deciduous (monsoon) forest is the most widespread in India, growing in moderate rainfall areas, with trees that shed leaves in the dry season.

stem: Which valuable timber tree is characteristic of the tropical deciduous (monsoon) forests of India?
solution: Teak (and sal) are the characteristic and valuable timber trees of the tropical deciduous (monsoon) forests of India. Teak is a prized hardwood (durable, used for furniture and construction), found especially in the deciduous forests of central and southern India; sal is another important deciduous hardwood, common in the forests of central and eastern India. Other trees of these forests include sandalwood, sheesham (rosewood), and mahua. These forests are the most commercially important in India because of such useful timbers. Understanding that teak and sal are characteristic of the deciduous forests is a prelims point. Teak (and sal) are the characteristic valuable timber trees of India's tropical deciduous forests.

stem: The vegetation found in the arid and semi-arid regions of India (like Rajasthan), consisting of thorny bushes, cacti, and hardy shrubs, is the __________ vegetation.
solution: The thorn forests and scrub vegetation are found in the arid and semi-arid regions of India — areas of low rainfall (generally less than about 70 cm a year) — such as Rajasthan, parts of Gujarat, Punjab, Haryana, and the rain-shadow areas of the Deccan. This vegetation consists of thorny trees and bushes, cacti, and hardy, drought-resistant shrubs (like acacia/babul, khejri, and various cacti and euphorbias). The plants are adapted to the dry conditions — with long roots, thick/waxy skin, small or spine-like leaves (to reduce water loss), and the ability to store water. Understanding the thorn/scrub vegetation of dry regions is a prelims point. Thorn (and scrub) vegetation — thorny bushes, cacti, and hardy shrubs — grows in the dry, arid regions of India.

stem: The salt-tolerant forests of the tidal, coastal, deltaic areas (like the Sundarbans), with special breathing roots, are the __________ forests.
solution: The mangrove forests (also called tidal or littoral forests) are the salt-tolerant forests found in the tidal, waterlogged, brackish (salty) coastal and deltaic areas — such as the deltas of the Ganga-Brahmaputra (the Sundarbans), the Godavari, the Krishna, and the Mahanadi, and other sheltered coasts. Mangrove trees have special adaptations to survive in the salty, muddy, waterlogged conditions — such as stilt/prop roots and breathing roots (pneumatophores, which stick up out of the mud to get oxygen). The Sundarbans (in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta) is the largest mangrove forest in the world. Mangroves protect the coast and are rich habitats. Understanding the mangrove (tidal) forests is a prelims point. Mangrove forests are the salt-tolerant tidal forests of coastal/deltaic areas, like the Sundarbans, with breathing roots.

stem: The type of vegetation found at high altitudes in the Himalayas (above the tree line), consisting of small shrubs, grasses, mosses, and lichens, is the __________ vegetation.
solution: The montane (mountain) vegetation, and at the highest levels the alpine vegetation, is found in the Himalayan mountains, and it changes with altitude (height): as one goes up, the vegetation changes from tropical/deciduous forests at the foot, to temperate forests (oak, pine, deodar, fir, spruce) higher up, to alpine forests and then alpine meadows (grasslands) still higher, and finally, above the tree line, to small alpine shrubs, grasses, mosses, and lichens (tundra-like vegetation), before the permanent snow. So mountain vegetation shows a vertical zonation (change with altitude), similar to the change one sees going from the equator to the poles. Understanding montane/alpine vegetation (changing with altitude in the Himalayas) is a prelims point. Montane/alpine vegetation is the high-altitude Himalayan vegetation (temperate forests up to alpine shrubs, grasses, and mosses).

stem: In the Himalayan mountains, the natural vegetation changes with __________ (just as it changes with latitude from the equator to the poles).
solution: In the Himalayan mountains, the natural vegetation changes with altitude (height above sea level) — a pattern called altitudinal (vertical) zonation. As one climbs higher, the temperature falls (about 6.5°C per km), so the vegetation changes in zones: tropical/deciduous forests at the base, then temperate forests (oak, pine, deodar/cedar, fir, spruce) at middle heights, then alpine forests and alpine meadows higher up, and finally alpine shrubs, grasses, and mosses above the tree line — before the permanent snow. This vertical change with altitude mirrors the horizontal change of vegetation one sees going from the hot equator toward the cold poles. Understanding that mountain vegetation changes with altitude is a prelims point. In the Himalayas, natural vegetation changes with altitude, in zones, just as it changes with latitude from the equator to the poles.

stem: The 'ecosystem' concept in the study of natural vegetation emphasises that plants, animals, and their environment are:
solution: The ecosystem concept emphasises that the plants (vegetation), the animals, and their physical environment (soil, water, climate) of an area are all interrelated and interdependent — linked together in a functioning system, through the flows of energy (food chains) and the cycling of nutrients. So the natural vegetation is not isolated: it depends on the environment, it supports the animal life, and disturbing one part (like cutting the forest) affects the whole ecosystem (the animals, the soil, the water, the climate). This ecological view underlies the importance of conserving vegetation and forests. Understanding the ecosystem concept (interdependence of plants, animals, environment) is a prelims point. The ecosystem concept stresses that plants, animals, and their environment are interrelated and interdependent.

stem: Forests are important because they provide many resources and benefits, such as:
options: Timber, fuel, fodder, medicines, and many other products, plus oxygen, wildlife habitat, and soil and water conservation
solution: Forests are extremely important because they provide many resources and benefits: they yield timber (wood for construction and furniture), fuel wood, fodder (for animals), bamboo, and a host of other products — medicines, gums, resins, lac, honey, fruits, and raw materials for many industries (paper, matches, etc.). Beyond products, forests perform vital ecological services: they release oxygen and absorb carbon dioxide (purifying the air and combating global warming); they are the habitat of wildlife (supporting biodiversity); they conserve soil (their roots prevent erosion) and water (they help rainwater soak in, recharging groundwater and regulating rivers); and they influence the climate and increase rainfall. This is why conserving forests is so important. Understanding the importance of forests is a prelims-relevant point. Forests provide timber, fuel, fodder, medicines, and many products, plus oxygen, wildlife habitat, and soil/water conservation.

stem: The clearing/cutting down of forests (for farming, timber, settlements, etc.), which is a major environmental problem in India, is called:
solution: Deforestation is the clearing or cutting down of forests — the removal of the natural forest cover — for purposes such as agriculture (clearing land for crops), timber/fuel wood, settlements, industry, mining, roads, and dams. Deforestation is a major environmental problem in India (and the world), because it causes: loss of forest resources and biodiversity (habitats and species); soil erosion and loss of soil fertility; disruption of the water cycle (reduced rainfall, floods, lower groundwater); and increased carbon dioxide (contributing to global warming). This is why controlling deforestation and undertaking afforestation are important. Understanding deforestation (the cutting down of forests) is a prelims point. Deforestation is the clearing/cutting down of forests, a major environmental problem in India.

stem: The planting of trees / growing of forests (to increase the forest cover) is called:
solution: Afforestation is the planting of trees and the growing/establishing of forests on land — especially on land that was not previously forested, or to increase the forest cover — done to make up for the loss of forests (deforestation) and to gain the benefits of forests. (The related term 'reforestation' means replanting forests on land that was recently deforested.) Afforestation helps to combat deforestation, soil erosion, and global warming (trees absorb CO2), and to restore the ecological benefits of forests. Programmes like 'Van Mahotsav' (a tree-planting festival) promote afforestation in India. Understanding afforestation (planting trees to grow forests) is a prelims point. Afforestation is the planting of trees/growing of forests to increase the forest cover.

stem: Areas set aside by the government to protect wildlife, where hunting is banned and animals are protected in their natural habitat, are called wildlife sanctuaries and:
solution: To protect wildlife (animals and their habitats), the government sets aside protected areas — chiefly wildlife sanctuaries and national parks — where hunting/poaching is banned and the animals and plants are protected in their natural habitat. (National parks are areas of strict protection reserved for wildlife, where even private activity is restricted; wildlife sanctuaries are also protected but may allow some regulated human activity.) In addition, 'biosphere reserves' protect whole ecosystems. India has many national parks (like Jim Corbett, Kaziranga) and sanctuaries, and special projects like 'Project Tiger' and 'Project Elephant' to protect particular endangered species. Understanding national parks and wildlife sanctuaries (protected areas for wildlife) is a prelims point. National parks and wildlife sanctuaries are protected areas set aside to protect wildlife in their natural habitat.

stem: The famous project launched in India to protect the tiger (an endangered national animal) is called:
solution: Project Tiger is the famous conservation project launched in India (in 1973) to protect the tiger — India's national animal and an endangered species — and its habitat. Under Project Tiger, special protected areas called 'tiger reserves' (like Jim Corbett, Bandhavgarh, Ranthambore, Sundarbans) were established, where tigers are protected from poaching and habitat loss, and their numbers are monitored and conserved. (A similar 'Project Elephant' protects elephants.) Project Tiger is an important example of India's wildlife conservation efforts. Understanding Project Tiger (for tiger conservation) is a prelims-relevant point. Project Tiger is the Indian project launched to protect the endangered tiger and its habitat.

stem: The tropical evergreen forests are found on the WESTERN slopes of the Western Ghats but not on the eastern (Deccan) side because:
options: The western (windward) slopes get very heavy rainfall, while the eastern (leeward) side lies in a rain shadow and is drier
There is no soil in the west
solution: The tropical evergreen forests grow on the western (windward) slopes of the Western Ghats but not on the eastern (Deccan) side because of the rainfall pattern: the western slopes face the moist Arabian Sea branch of the monsoon and receive very heavy rainfall (over 200 cm) — enough for the dense evergreen rainforest; while the eastern side lies in the rain shadow (leeward side) of the Ghats and receives much less rain, so it can support only deciduous or drier forests, not the moisture-loving evergreen forest. This shows how vegetation follows rainfall. Understanding this rain-shadow effect on vegetation is a prelims point. Evergreen forests grow on the wet western slopes of the Western Ghats, not the drier eastern (rain-shadow) side.

stem: The natural vegetation of India is highly diverse because of the country's great diversity of:
solution: The natural vegetation of India is highly diverse (varied) because of the country's great diversity of physical conditions — especially its relief (from the high Himalayas to the coastal plains), its climate (a wide range of rainfall — from the very wet north-east and west coast to the arid Thar — and of temperature — from the tropical south to the cold high mountains), and its varied soils. Since vegetation depends on these physical conditions, India's wide range of relief, climate, and soils gives rise to a wide range of natural vegetation — from tropical rainforests and deciduous forests to thorn/desert vegetation, mangroves, and alpine vegetation. Understanding why India's vegetation is diverse (diverse relief/climate/soils) is a prelims point. India's natural vegetation is diverse because of its great diversity of relief, climate, and soils.

stem: Plants of the desert/arid regions (like the cactus and thorny acacia) are adapted to dry conditions with features such as:
options: Broad, thin leaves and shallow roots
Long roots, thick/waxy stems that store water, and small or spine-like leaves (to reduce water loss)
solution: Plants of the desert and arid regions (like cacti and thorny acacia/babul) are adapted to survive the dry conditions (scarce water and intense heat) with special features such as: long roots that go deep (or spread wide) to reach water; thick, fleshy, waxy stems that store water (in cacti); small, thick, waxy, or spine-like leaves (or no leaves — the spines) to reduce the loss of water by transpiration; and a thick, protective bark/skin. These adaptations (which make such plants 'xerophytes') let them conserve water and survive where rainfall is very low. Understanding the adaptations of desert plants is a prelims point. Desert plants are adapted with long roots, water-storing thick stems, and small/spine-like leaves to reduce water loss.

stem: The forests where trees shed their leaves in the dry season to conserve water are called deciduous forests. The word 'deciduous' means:
solution: The word 'deciduous' means leaf-shedding — that is, the trees shed (drop) their leaves seasonally (in these forests, during the dry season). The deciduous (monsoon) forests do this to conserve water: by dropping their leaves in the dry season, the trees reduce the loss of water through the leaves (transpiration) at the time when water is scarce, and they grow new leaves when the rains return. This is in contrast to 'evergreen' forests, which stay green all year (never appearing bare). Understanding that 'deciduous' means leaf-shedding is a prelims point. 'Deciduous' means leaf-shedding — deciduous forests drop their leaves in the dry season to conserve water.

stem: Assertion (A): Mangrove forests can survive in salty, waterlogged coastal mud. Reason (R): Mangroves have special adaptations, such as breathing roots (that get oxygen from the air) and salt-tolerance. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that mangrove forests can survive in the salty, waterlogged, muddy conditions of tidal coastal/deltaic areas. And the reason is (R) that mangroves have special adaptations that make this possible — notably breathing roots (pneumatophores), which grow upward out of the waterlogged mud to take in oxygen from the air (since the mud is oxygen-poor), and salt-tolerance (special ways to cope with or excrete the excess salt), as well as stilt/prop roots for support in the soft mud. These adaptations are exactly what allow mangroves to live where ordinary plants cannot — so R correctly explains A. Understanding the adaptations of mangroves is a prelims point. Mangroves survive in salty, waterlogged mud because of adaptations like breathing roots and salt-tolerance.

stem: The tropical deciduous forests are divided into moist deciduous and dry deciduous. The MOIST deciduous forests grow in areas of __________ rainfall than the dry deciduous forests.
solution: The tropical deciduous (monsoon) forests are divided into two sub-types based on rainfall: the moist deciduous forests grow in areas of higher rainfall (about 100–200 cm), and the dry deciduous forests grow in areas of lower rainfall (about 70–100 cm). The moist deciduous forests (with more rain) are denser and have more valuable timber (like teak, sal, sandalwood); the dry deciduous forests (with less rain), found in the drier interior, are more open and merge into scrub/thorn vegetation as rainfall decreases. Understanding that moist deciduous forests get more rain than dry deciduous is a prelims point. Moist deciduous forests grow in areas of higher rainfall than the dry deciduous forests.

stem: The mangrove tree that gives its name to the Sundarbans (the largest mangrove forest, in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta) is the:
solution: The Sundari tree (a mangrove species) gives its name to the Sundarbans — the largest mangrove forest in the world, in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta (West Bengal and Bangladesh). The name 'Sundarbans' is derived from the Sundari trees that grow there in abundance. The Sundarbans is a rich mangrove ecosystem and the famous habitat of the Royal Bengal Tiger. Understanding that the Sundari tree names the Sundarbans is a prelims point. The Sundari tree gives its name to the Sundarbans mangrove forest.

stem: Valuable timber trees like rosewood, mahogany, and ebony are characteristic of which forest type?
solution: Rosewood, mahogany, and ebony are hardwood trees characteristic of the tropical evergreen (rainforest) forests of India (which grow in the very-heavy-rainfall areas of the Western Ghats, the north-east, and the Andamans). These forests are rich in tall, valuable hardwood trees (though they are harder to exploit than the deciduous forests, because of the difficult terrain and mixed species). (By contrast, teak and sal are characteristic of the deciduous forests; acacia/babul of the thorn forests; and deodar/pine of the montane forests.) Understanding that rosewood, mahogany, and ebony belong to the evergreen forests is a prelims point. Rosewood, mahogany, and ebony are characteristic trees of the tropical evergreen forests.

stem: According to the National Forest Policy, the ideal proportion of India's area that should be under forest cover is about:
solution: According to India's National Forest Policy, the ideal/desirable proportion of the country's total geographical area that should be under forest (and tree) cover is about 33% (one-third) — with a higher proportion (about 60%) recommended for the hills and mountains (to protect the fragile slopes and water sources) and about 33% for the plains. This target is set to maintain ecological balance and to meet the country's needs. In reality, India's actual forest cover is well below this ideal (around 21–24%), which is why afforestation is emphasised. Understanding the 33% forest-cover target is a prelims point. The National Forest Policy recommends about 33% (one-third) of India's area under forest cover.

stem: The actual forest cover of India is currently around __________ of its geographical area (below the recommended one-third).
solution: The actual forest cover of India is currently around 21–24% of its total geographical area (roughly one-fifth to a little under a quarter) — which is well below the one-third (33%) recommended by the National Forest Policy. This shortfall (and the pressures of deforestation from a growing population, agriculture, and development) is why increasing the forest cover through afforestation and conservation is an important goal in India. Understanding India's actual forest cover (~21–24%, below the target) is a prelims-relevant point. India's actual forest cover is around 21–24% of its area, below the recommended one-third.

stem: The famous grassroots movement in which villagers (led by women) hugged trees to prevent them from being cut down, in the Himalayan region, was the __________ movement.
solution: The Chipko movement was the famous grassroots environmental movement (in the 1970s, in the Himalayan region of Uttarakhand — then part of Uttar Pradesh) in which villagers, especially women, hugged (embraced) the trees to physically prevent them from being cut down by contractors. ('Chipko' means 'to hug/stick to'.) It was a powerful non-violent protest to protect the forests (on which the villagers' lives depended), and it became a symbol of community-based forest conservation and the wider environmental movement in India. Understanding the Chipko movement (tree-hugging to save forests) is a prelims-relevant point. The Chipko movement was the tree-hugging movement in the Himalayas to prevent trees from being cut down.

stem: The practice in which local communities and the forest department jointly manage and protect forests (sharing the responsibility and benefits) is called:
solution: Joint Forest Management (JFM) is the approach/programme in which the local communities (villagers living in and around forests) and the forest department work together (jointly) to manage, protect, and regenerate the forests — sharing both the responsibility of protecting the forest and the benefits (forest produce) from it. JFM recognises that involving and benefiting the local people is essential for successful forest conservation (since they depend on the forests). It has been an important strategy for community-based forest protection in India. Understanding Joint Forest Management (community + department managing forests) is a prelims-relevant point. Joint Forest Management (JFM) is the joint management of forests by local communities and the forest department.

stem: Patches of forest traditionally protected by local communities for religious/cultural reasons (dedicated to deities, where cutting is forbidden) are called:
solution: Sacred groves are patches or tracts of forest (or a cluster of trees) that are traditionally protected and preserved by local communities for religious and cultural reasons — often dedicated to a local deity or ancestral spirit, where the cutting of trees and the killing of animals are forbidden (taboo). Because they are protected by these traditional beliefs, sacred groves often preserve rich, undisturbed natural vegetation and rare species (they act as tiny nature reserves). They are found in many parts of India (with different local names). Understanding sacred groves (community-protected sacred forest patches) is a prelims-relevant point. Sacred groves are forest patches traditionally protected by communities for religious reasons, where cutting is forbidden.

stem: The very heavy rainfall and warm climate of the north-eastern states and the Western Ghats make them regions of very high __________ (variety of plant and animal life).
solution: The very heavy rainfall and warm, humid climate of the north-eastern states and the Western Ghats make them regions of very high biodiversity (a great variety and richness of plant and animal species). These wet, warm conditions support dense evergreen rainforests, which harbour an enormous variety of life. In fact, the Western Ghats and the north-eastern Himalayas/Indo-Burma region are recognised as global 'biodiversity hotspots' (areas of exceptional biodiversity that are also under threat). Understanding that the wet north-east and Western Ghats have high biodiversity is a prelims-relevant point. The heavy rainfall of the north-east and the Western Ghats makes them regions of very high biodiversity.

stem: The Western Ghats, the Himalayas, and the Indo-Burma (north-east) region are recognised as global __________ — areas of exceptional biodiversity that are also threatened.
solution: The Western Ghats, the Himalayas, and the Indo-Burma (north-eastern) region (and the Sundaland region, which includes the Nicobar Islands) are recognised as global biodiversity hotspots — areas that have an exceptional richness of biodiversity (many species, including many endemic ones found nowhere else) but that are also under serious threat from human activities (habitat destruction). Biodiversity hotspots are priority areas for conservation. India, with these hotspots, is one of the world's biologically rich ('megadiverse') countries. Understanding India's biodiversity hotspots (Western Ghats, Himalaya, Indo-Burma) is a prelims-relevant point. The Western Ghats, the Himalayas, and the Indo-Burma region are recognised as global biodiversity hotspots.

stem: The famous national park in Assam that is home to the great one-horned rhinoceros is:
solution: Kaziranga National Park, in Assam (in the Brahmaputra floodplain), is famous as the home of the great one-horned rhinoceros (Indian rhinoceros) — it protects the largest population of this endangered species in the world. Kaziranga (a World Heritage Site) also has tigers, elephants, wild water buffalo, and many birds. Understanding that Kaziranga (Assam) protects the one-horned rhino is a prelims point. Kaziranga National Park, in Assam, is home to the great one-horned rhinoceros.

stem: The only home of the Asiatic lion in India is the __________ National Park/forest in Gujarat.
solution: The Gir National Park (Gir Forest) in Gujarat is the only home (natural habitat) of the Asiatic lion in India (and in the world) — the last surviving population of Asiatic lions lives in and around Gir. This makes Gir extremely important for the conservation of this endangered species. Understanding that Gir (Gujarat) is the home of the Asiatic lion is a prelims point. The Gir National Park in Gujarat is the only home of the Asiatic lion.

stem: The first biosphere reserve established in India (in the Western Ghats region) is the __________ Biosphere Reserve.
solution: The Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve (in the Western Ghats, spanning parts of Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Karnataka) was the first biosphere reserve established in India (in 1986). Biosphere reserves are large protected areas set up to conserve the whole ecosystem — the plants, animals, and their habitat — along with the traditional life of the local people. India now has many biosphere reserves (like the Sundarbans, Nanda Devi, Gulf of Mannar, etc.), but the Nilgiri was the first. Understanding that the Nilgiri was India's first biosphere reserve is a prelims point. The Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve (in the Western Ghats) was the first biosphere reserve established in India.

stem: The law enacted in India in 1972 to protect wild animals, birds, and plants is the:
solution: The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 is the major law enacted in India to protect wild animals, birds, and plants and their habitats. It provides for the protection of listed (scheduled) species (banning their hunting/poaching and trade), and for the establishment of protected areas such as national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, and (later) conservation and community reserves. It is the legal foundation of wildlife conservation in India. Understanding the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 is a prelims-relevant point. The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 is the Indian law to protect wild animals, birds, and plants.

stem: The annual tree-planting festival/programme promoted in India to encourage afforestation is called:
solution: Van Mahotsav (meaning 'forest festival') is the annual tree-planting festival/programme in India (usually held in July), during which large numbers of trees are planted across the country to promote afforestation, increase the green cover, and raise awareness about the importance of trees and forests. It is one of India's efforts to combat deforestation and encourage people to plant and protect trees. Understanding Van Mahotsav (the tree-planting festival) is a prelims-relevant point. Van Mahotsav is the annual tree-planting festival promoted in India to encourage afforestation.

stem: The important coniferous tree of the Himalayan montane forests, prized for its timber (and the state tree of Himachal Pradesh), is the:
solution: The Deodar (Himalayan cedar) is an important, tall coniferous (evergreen needle-leaf) tree of the Himalayan montane (temperate) forests. It is prized for its strong, durable, fragrant timber (used in construction), and it is the state tree of Himachal Pradesh. Other conifers of the Himalayan forests include pine, fir, and spruce. (The deodar grows at the middle/higher altitudes of the western Himalayas.) Understanding the deodar (Himalayan conifer, prized timber) is a prelims point. The Deodar (Himalayan cedar) is a prized coniferous timber tree of the Himalayan montane forests.

stem: Deforestation leads to increased soil __________, because the tree roots that used to bind the soil are removed.
solution: Deforestation leads to increased soil erosion, because when the forest is cleared, the tree roots (which used to bind and hold the soil together) and the leafy cover (which used to protect the soil from the direct impact of rain and shade it) are removed — so the bare soil is easily washed away by rain (and blown away by wind). This soil erosion strips away the fertile topsoil, reduces the land's productivity, silts up rivers and reservoirs, and can lead to floods and landslides. So deforestation and soil erosion are closely linked — a key reason for protecting forests. Understanding that deforestation causes soil erosion is a prelims point. Deforestation increases soil erosion, because the tree roots that bound the soil (and the protective cover) are removed.

stem: Forests are considered a __________ natural resource, because they can be regrown/renewed (if managed sustainably).
solution: Forests are considered a renewable natural resource, because — unlike minerals or fossil fuels (which are non-renewable and get used up permanently) — forests can be regrown, renewed, and replenished: trees can be replanted and forests can regenerate (grow back) over time, if they are used and managed wisely and sustainably (not cut faster than they can regrow). This is why sustainable forest management and afforestation can keep forests as a lasting resource. (However, if forests are over-exploited or destroyed faster than they regrow, they can be lost — so 'renewable' depends on careful management.) Understanding that forests are a renewable resource is a prelims point. Forests are a renewable natural resource, because they can be regrown and renewed if managed sustainably.

stem: Wetlands (marshes, lakes, mangroves) of international importance in India are protected under the __________ Convention.
solution: Wetlands (such as marshes, lakes, lagoons, and mangroves) of international importance are protected under the Ramsar Convention — an international treaty (named after the city of Ramsar in Iran, where it was signed in 1971) for the conservation and wise use of wetlands. Wetlands designated under this convention are called 'Ramsar sites'. India has many Ramsar sites (like Chilika Lake, Wular Lake, Keoladeo/Bharatpur, and the Sundarbans). Wetlands are valuable ecosystems — rich in biodiversity, important for water, fisheries, and migratory birds. Understanding the Ramsar Convention (protecting wetlands) is a prelims-relevant point. Wetlands of international importance are protected under the Ramsar Convention (as 'Ramsar sites').

stem: Forests help to reduce global warming because they:
options: Absorb carbon dioxide (and release oxygen) through photosynthesis, acting as carbon sinks
solution: Forests help to reduce global warming because they absorb carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere — the main greenhouse gas — and release oxygen, through the process of photosynthesis. By taking in and storing carbon (in their trees, plants, and soil), forests act as 'carbon sinks', reducing the amount of CO2 in the air and thus helping to slow global warming. (This is a key reason why deforestation is harmful — it not only removes this CO2-absorbing sink but also releases the stored carbon — and why afforestation helps fight climate change.) Understanding that forests absorb CO2 (carbon sinks) and reduce global warming is a prelims-relevant point. Forests reduce global warming by absorbing carbon dioxide (and releasing oxygen), acting as carbon sinks.

stem: The khejri tree, well adapted to the desert and greatly valued (the state tree of Rajasthan), is characteristic of which vegetation type?
solution: The khejri tree is characteristic of the thorn (desert/arid) vegetation of India's dry regions (like Rajasthan). It is a hardy, drought-resistant tree, extremely well adapted to the desert (with deep roots to reach underground water), and it is greatly valued by the people of Rajasthan for its many uses (fodder, fuel, food, shade) — so much so that it is the state tree of Rajasthan (and was famously protected by the Bishnoi community, who gave their lives to save khejri trees). Understanding that the khejri belongs to the thorn/desert vegetation is a prelims point. The khejri tree is characteristic of the thorn (desert/arid) vegetation of Rajasthan.

stem: The natural vegetation also changes with the SOIL: for example, mangroves grow in salty coastal mud, and certain plants grow only on particular soils. This shows that, besides climate, __________ also influences vegetation.
solution: Besides climate (the chief control), the soil also influences the natural vegetation of a place — different soils support different plants. For example, mangroves grow in the salty, waterlogged coastal/deltaic mud; certain grasses and plants grow on the black soil, others on sandy or rocky soils; and the depth, texture, moisture, and mineral content of the soil affect which plants can grow. (Along with soil, relief/altitude and drainage also influence vegetation.) So the natural vegetation of an area reflects not just its climate but also its soil (and other physical conditions). Understanding that soil (besides climate) influences vegetation is a prelims point. Soil (besides climate) also influences natural vegetation — different soils support different plants.

stem: The Himalayan vegetation, going up in altitude, changes roughly in the order:
options: Alpine meadows → temperate forests → tropical forests
Tropical/deciduous forests → temperate (pine, deodar, fir) forests → alpine forests and meadows → snow
solution: The Himalayan (montane) vegetation changes with increasing altitude roughly in this order (from the foot to the top): tropical/deciduous forests at the lowest levels (the foothills); then, higher up, sub-tropical and temperate forests (evergreen oaks, chestnut, and conifers like pine, deodar, fir, and spruce); then, still higher, alpine forests and alpine meadows (grasslands); and finally, above the tree line, small alpine shrubs, grasses, mosses, and lichens — up to the line of permanent snow. So the vegetation zones change from tropical at the base to alpine/tundra-like near the top, reflecting the fall in temperature with height. Understanding this altitudinal sequence of Himalayan vegetation is a prelims point. Himalayan vegetation changes with altitude: tropical/deciduous → temperate (pine, deodar, fir) → alpine forests and meadows → snow.

stem: The Keoladeo Ghana National Park (Bharatpur, Rajasthan), a famous Ramsar wetland, is especially important as a habitat for:
solution: The Keoladeo Ghana National Park (in Bharatpur, Rajasthan) is a famous wetland (a Ramsar site and World Heritage Site) especially important as a habitat and wintering ground for a great many migratory birds — including numerous water birds that travel there from distant regions (historically even the rare Siberian crane). It is one of India's most renowned bird sanctuaries. This illustrates the importance of wetlands for bird life and biodiversity. Understanding that Keoladeo (Bharatpur) is famous for migratory birds is a prelims-relevant point. The Keoladeo Ghana National Park (Bharatpur) is famous as a habitat for migratory birds.

stem: The tropical thorn forests and scrub are found where the annual rainfall is generally less than about:
solution: The tropical thorn forests and scrub are found in the semi-arid and arid regions where the annual rainfall is generally less than about 70 cm (and especially below 50 cm) — such as western Rajasthan, and parts of Gujarat, Punjab, Haryana, and the rain-shadow interior of the Deccan. In these low-rainfall conditions, only drought-adapted thorny trees, bushes, cacti, and hardy shrubs can grow. (As a rough guide to India's forests by rainfall: over 200 cm → evergreen; 100–200 cm → moist deciduous; 70–100 cm → dry deciduous; below 70 cm → thorn/scrub.) Understanding that thorn forests occur below ~70 cm of rainfall is a prelims point. Tropical thorn forests and scrub occur where the annual rainfall is generally less than about 70 cm.

stem: The 'Red Data Book' is a record that lists:
options: The rare and endangered/threatened species of plants and animals
solution: The 'Red Data Book' (or Red List) is a record/document that lists the rare, threatened, and endangered species of plants and animals (species at risk of extinction), maintained to keep track of their status and to focus conservation efforts on them. (The international Red List is maintained by the IUCN — the International Union for Conservation of Nature.) It categorises species by how threatened they are (e.g., vulnerable, endangered, critically endangered, extinct). Understanding the Red Data Book (record of endangered species) is a prelims-relevant point. The Red Data Book lists the rare and endangered/threatened species of plants and animals.

stem: The programme of growing trees and forests on community/waste lands and along roads, canals, and railways to meet local needs (fuel, fodder) is called:
solution: Social forestry is the programme/practice of growing trees and forests on community lands, waste lands, and along roadsides, canal banks, and railway lines — as well as on farms — mainly to meet the local people's needs for fuel wood, fodder (for animals), small timber, and other products, and to improve the environment (green cover, soil conservation). By involving the community and providing these everyday needs, social forestry aims to reduce the pressure on the natural forests and to increase the tree cover. (A related idea, 'agroforestry', grows trees together with crops on farmland.) Understanding social forestry (community tree-growing for local needs) is a prelims-relevant point. Social forestry is the growing of trees on community/waste lands and roadsides to meet local needs for fuel and fodder.

stem: Which of the following is an example of the ADAPTATION of vegetation to its environment?
options: Thick, waxy, spiny leaves and water-storing stems in desert plants; buttressed roots and drip-tip leaves in rainforest trees; breathing roots in mangroves
solution: Plants adapt to (are suited to) the conditions of their environment, and their features reflect this. Examples of such adaptation include: desert plants with thick, waxy, or spiny (reduced) leaves and water-storing stems and deep roots (to survive drought); tropical rainforest trees with buttressed (supporting) roots, and leaves with 'drip tips' (to shed the heavy rain); and mangroves with breathing roots (pneumatophores) and salt-tolerance (to survive the salty, waterlogged mud). Each type of vegetation is thus adapted to its particular climate and site. (A cactus would not naturally grow in a rainforest, nor a mangrove in the desert — each grows where it is adapted.) Understanding vegetation adaptation to the environment is a prelims point. Vegetation adapts to its environment — e.g., spiny water-storing desert plants, drip-tip rainforest leaves, and breathing-rooted mangroves.

stem: Assertion (A): The north-eastern region of India has very rich and dense forests. Reason (R): The north-east has a warm climate with very heavy rainfall, ideal for the growth of dense, varied vegetation. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the north-eastern region of India has very rich, dense, and varied forests (with high biodiversity). And the reason is (R) that the north-east has a warm (tropical/subtropical) climate combined with very heavy rainfall (it includes some of the wettest places on Earth) — conditions that are ideal for the luxuriant growth of dense, varied vegetation (evergreen rainforests). Because vegetation depends chiefly on climate (warmth and rainfall), the warm, very wet climate of the north-east is exactly why it has such rich, dense forests — so R correctly explains A. Understanding this climate-vegetation link for the north-east is a prelims point. The north-east has rich, dense forests because its warm climate and very heavy rainfall are ideal for dense, varied vegetation.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Natural Vegetation' (of India) is that:
options: India has only one type of vegetation

India has a rich diversity of natural vegetation — tropical evergreen, deciduous (monsoon), thorn, mangrove (tidal), and montane (mountain) types — determined mainly by climate (rainfall and temperature) and relief; this vegetation is a valuable resource (and part of the ecosystem) that must be conserved against deforestation
Vegetation is not affected by climate
solution: The chapter conveys that India has a rich diversity of natural vegetation, determined mainly by the climate (especially rainfall and temperature) and the relief/altitude, and classified into several major types: the tropical evergreen (rainforest) forests of the very-heavy-rainfall areas (the western Ghats, the north-east, the Andamans), which are dense and green all year; the tropical deciduous (monsoon) forests of the moderate-rainfall areas — the most widespread and economically important, with valuable timbers like teak and sal, whose trees shed their leaves in the dry season; the thorn forests and scrub of the dry, arid regions (like Rajasthan), with drought-adapted thorny plants and cacti; the mangrove (tidal) forests of the salty, waterlogged coastal deltas (like the Sundarbans), with special breathing roots; and the montane (mountain) vegetation of the Himalayas, which changes with altitude (from deciduous and temperate forests up to alpine meadows and shrubs). It stresses that this natural vegetation is a valuable resource — providing timber, fuel, fodder, medicines, and many products, and vital ecological services (oxygen, wildlife habitat, soil and water conservation, climate regulation) — and an integral part of the ecosystem (interlinked with animals and the environment); and that it is threatened by deforestation, so it must be protected and increased through conservation, afforestation, and the protection of wildlife (national parks, sanctuaries, Project Tiger). Understanding the types of natural vegetation, their climatic basis, their importance, and their conservation is the central concern of this chapter. India has diverse natural vegetation — evergreen, deciduous, thorn, mangrove, and montane types — shaped by climate and relief, and a valuable resource to be conserved.
